\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large-scale LLM serving is increasingly shaped by the convergence of two trends that are independently effective but jointly challenging: sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) base models~\cite{todo:moe-llm} and LoRA-based adaptation~\cite{todo:lora-original,todo:lora-serving}. In production prefill--decode (PD) deployments~\cite{todo:pd-serving}, this combination places particular stress on the decode stage. Decode is latency-sensitive, operates at small effective batch sizes, and repeats routing and parameter-management decisions once per generated token. Consequently, inefficiencies that are amortized in prefill directly translate into increased per-token latency and, more critically, amplified P99 tail latency in decode.

Existing systems are not designed for this regime because they organize around abstractions that do not align with its access pattern. In pure MoE serving, the natural unit of management is the expert. In multi-LoRA serving, the unit is the adapter. Prior systems such as S-LoRA and VaLoRA~\cite{todo:slora,todo:valora} therefore adopt adapter-centric designs. However, in MoE + multi-LoRA decode, a request only requires the LoRA residual associated with the \emph{selected experts}. The true unit of reuse is thus a joint expert--adapter object, rather than an expert-only or adapter-only entity. This shift fundamentally changes the locality structure: the joint key space expands the working set, fragments reuse, and makes GPU residency significantly harder to sustain under fixed memory budgets.

Our trace-driven case study shows that this is not a marginal effect but a regime shift. When accesses are modeled using joint keys, the top 1000 objects account for only 40.7\% and 32.6\% of accesses under independent and correlated adapter mappings, compared to 89.1\% under expert-only modeling. Temporal locality degrades accordingly: the finite P99 reuse distance increases from 1,393 events to 2,041 and 4,521 events, while cold first touches rise from 1.0 to 9.7 and 13.6 per 10k events. These results demonstrate that multi-LoRA does not merely increase parameter count; it drives the system into a more fragmented and less cache-friendly locality regime.

This fragmentation translates directly into system-level degradation under realistic cache budgets. With a shared 2048-object LRU cache, the miss rate increases from 0.00159 (expert-only) to 0.01095 and 0.01476 under joint-key modeling, a 6.9$\times$--9.3$\times$ increase. While the absolute miss rate remains low, these misses are highly skewed and concentrate on tail requests, where even a small number of misses directly dominate P99 latency. In this regime, performance is governed not by average miss rate, but by the worst-case accumulation of cold-object accesses. Synthetic control sweeps further show that the tail penalty emerges early and persists: at a fixed cache slice, the P99 latency proxy rises sharply as the number of LoRAs increases and quickly plateaus at a high level. At the request level, tail latency is dominated not by average degradation but by bursts of cold-object accesses: while an average request touches tens of cold objects, tail requests may touch hundreds to over a thousand. These findings suggest that cache misses in this regime are not rare anomalies but \emph{structural events} concentrated on tail requests.

Once misses become structural, the conventional load-then-run paradigm becomes suboptimal. Existing GPU-centric systems treat a cache miss as a weight-migration problem, resolving it by transferring parameters from host to device before execution~\cite{todo:gpu-offload}. This paradigm works well for hot objects with predictable reuse, but breaks down for long-tail decode misses, where batches are small, reuse is uncertain, and host--device transfer latency is directly exposed on the critical path. The core bottleneck thus shifts from miss avoidance alone to \emph{miss handling}, requiring systems to decide how a miss should be served rather than simply how it should be avoided.

This paper presents \textbf{COLoRA}, a decode-worker runtime built around a \emph{dual-path execution paradigm} for handling cache misses. Instead of treating a miss as a mandatory weight-migration event, COLoRA treats it as a runtime execution choice between heterogeneous paths. 
COLoRA maintains (1) a bounded GPU hot cache for reusable joint objects and (2) a CPU-resident full replica. On a cache hit, execution follows the fast GPU path. On a miss, COLoRA selectively executes the LoRA residual via a CPU fallback path, primarily targeting cold, long-tail objects where GPU promotion is unlikely to amortize its cost, while optionally promoting the object asynchronously when reuse is likely. Importantly, this fallback path is overlapped with GPU execution to minimize exposed latency and is invoked only when beneficial, preventing it from becoming a dominant cost on the critical path.
To further reduce exposed latency, COLoRA incorporates a \emph{temporal-locality-guided speculative dispatch} mechanism that overlaps GPU execution with CPU fallback and data movement, minimizing idle bubbles in the decode pipeline. Together, these components transform miss handling from a blocking data-movement pipeline into a flexible execution-scheduling problem.

The key contributions of this work are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Problem characterization.} We identify the joint-object fragmentation regime in MoE multi-LoRA decode serving and show that the dominant failure mode is tail amplification from structural misses rather than uniform slowdown.
\item \textbf{Execution paradigm.} We introduce a dual-path execution model that treats cache misses as runtime execution choices rather than mandatory weight-migration events.
\item \textbf{System realization.} We design COLoRA, a heterogeneous runtime that integrates CPU fallback execution, temporal-locality-guided speculative dispatch, and selective asynchronous promotion to efficiently realize this paradigm.
\end{itemize}


\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{Serving Setting and System Boundary}
\label{subsec:setting}

We study decode execution within a single worker, where MoE routing and multi-LoRA adaptation interact to produce highly fragmented parameter access.
At this level, resource contention becomes explicit: GPU memory must simultaneously accommodate KV cache, backbone execution, and dynamically accessed LoRA residuals under heterogeneous and time-varying request patterns.

We therefore focus on this local execution context and do not consider cluster-level routing or global placement. The resulting fragmentation arises within individual decode steps and cannot be alleviated by higher-level scheduling, making it a fundamentally local systems problem.

\subsection{Joint Expert--Adapter as the Natural Management Unit}
\label{subsec:joint-object}

The key question is what the system should treat as the unit of management.

In dense models with a single adapter, adapter-level management suffices because most tokens share the same adapted weights. In MoE models, however, each token activates only a small routed subset of experts. With multiple adapters, accesses concentrate on LoRA residuals tied to specific expert--adapter pairs, rather than entire adapters or experts.

This leads to a necessary abstraction: the system must operate at the granularity of joint expert--adapter objects to accurately capture access behavior. Adapter-level management is too coarse, retaining many unused expert slices, while expert-level management is incomplete, ignoring adapter diversity and overestimating reuse.

In COLoRA, this abstraction is materialized as projection-specific cache entries keyed by (\mathit{projection}, \mathit{adapter}, \mathit{layer}, \mathit{expert}).

\subsection{Joint Objects Fragment Decode Locality}
\label{subsec:case-study}

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.49\textwidth]{figures/fig1_popularity_rank.pdf}
  \includegraphics[width=0.49\textwidth]{figures/fig2_reuse_distance.pdf}
  \caption{
  Joint expert--adapter modeling fundamentally degrades locality.\\
  (a) Popularity becomes significantly less concentrated: the top-1000 objects account for 89.1\% of accesses under expert-only modeling, but only 40.7\% and 32.6\% under joint modeling.\\
  (b) Temporal locality weakens: reuse distance increases substantially (P99: 1,393 → 2,041 → 4,521), and cold-start frequency rises sharply.\\
  Together, these results show that introducing the adapter dimension fragments both spatial and temporal locality, reducing the effectiveness of any bounded cache.
  }
  \label{fig:locality}
\end{figure*}

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.49\textwidth]{figures/fig3_cache_curve.pdf}
  \includegraphics[width=0.49\textwidth]{figures/fig5_tail_breakdown.pdf}
  \caption{
  Locality degradation directly translates into system-level inefficiency.\\
  (a) Under the same cache budget, miss rates increase significantly with joint modeling, showing that degraded locality cannot be compensated by fixed-capacity caching.\\
  (b) Tail requests access up to an order of magnitude more cold objects than average requests, concentrating misses in the tail.\\
  These results demonstrate that locality collapse not only increases average miss rate, but also amplifies tail latency.
  }
  \label{fig:system}
\end{figure*}
We establish the failure mode via trace-driven replay on a fixed MoE routing trace under three object definitions:
\texttt{B0} uses expert-only keys $(\mathit{layer}, \mathit{expert})$.
\texttt{B1} uses joint keys $(\mathit{layer}, \mathit{expert}, \mathit{adapter})$ with adapter identity sampled independently of expert routing.
\texttt{B2} uses the same joint keys under correlated assignment, where certain adapters are more likely to co-occur with specific experts.

Figures~\ref{fig:locality} and~\ref{fig:system} illustrate a two-stage failure: joint-object modeling first fragments locality, which then translates into higher miss rates and tail latency.

\paragraph{Popularity becomes less concentrated.}
As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:locality}(a), joint keys significantly flatten the popularity distribution: the top 1000 objects account for 89.1\% of accesses under expert-only modeling, but only 40.7\% and 32.6\% under joint modeling. The hot set therefore becomes less dominant, reducing the effectiveness of any bounded GPU cache.

\paragraph{Temporal locality weakens in the tail.}
Fig.~\ref{fig:locality}(b) shows that joint modeling increases reuse distance and cold-start frequency. The P99 reuse distance grows from 1{,}393 to 2{,}041 and 4{,}521 events, while cold first touches also rise substantially. These effects concentrate in the tail, where long reuse distances directly translate into latency spikes.

\paragraph{Locality loss amplifies misses and tail latency.}
As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:system}(a), miss rates increase significantly under the same cache budget. More importantly, Fig.~\ref{fig:system}(b) shows that tail requests access up to an order of magnitude more cold objects than average requests. Locality degradation therefore not only increases average miss rate, but also concentrates misses in tail requests, amplifying tail latency.

These results imply that locality degradation is inherent to joint-object modeling and cannot be effectively mitigated by cache scaling alone.

\section{Challenges}
\label{sec:challenges}

The above observations reveal a fundamental shift in the role of caching. 
Under joint-object modeling, locality degradation makes cache misses both frequent and concentrated in the tail, implying that misses are no longer rare events to be hidden, but a dominant factor that must be explicitly managed.

This reframes the problem: instead of minimizing misses, the system must decide how to handle unavoidable misses in a latency-critical decode path. Turning this insight into a practical runtime requires addressing three challenges.

\subsection{Challenge 1: Fine-Grained Residency Without Runaway Churn}
\label{subsec:challenge-residency}

Joint-object modeling flattens the popularity distribution, weakening the dominance of any small hot set. This makes coarse-grained residency ineffective, but fine-grained management introduces a new problem: a rapidly expanding key space with unstable reuse.

Naively caching at joint-object granularity leads to frequent insertions of low-reuse objects, repeated evictions, and wasted bandwidth on objects that never become hot again. The system must therefore preserve fine-grained precision while suppressing low-value promotions and avoiding repeated re-admission of cold objects. Otherwise, the cache degenerates into churn rather than improving locality.

\subsection{Challenge 2: Handling Misses Without Blocking the Critical Path}
\label{subsec:challenge-miss}

In this regime, many misses correspond to low-reuse objects whose cost cannot be amortized. Temporal locality weakens in the tail, causing reuse distances to grow and cold accesses to increase. As a result, many misses correspond to objects that are unlikely to be reused in the near future.

In this regime, the traditional load-then-run strategy becomes inefficient: blocking on weight transfer for low-reuse objects directly translates into tail latency. The system must therefore provide an alternative miss-handling path that can serve cold objects without stalling the decode pipeline, while keeping the fixed cost of this path low enough to remain competitive at small, irregular batch sizes.

\subsection{Challenge 3: Overlapping Heterogeneous Execution Without Creating a New Tail}
\label{subsec:challenge-overlap}

Locality loss not only increases miss frequency, but also concentrates misses in tail requests, making miss handling itself a latency-critical component.

A dual-path design introduces new interactions between GPU execution, CPU execution, and host--device transfers. If GPU execution stalls on every miss, the system collapses back into a serialized pipeline. Conversely, if fallback processing becomes overloaded, it becomes a new tail bottleneck.

The system must therefore overlap GPU hits with miss handling whenever dependencies allow, while controlling queueing and resource contention so that the tail remains predictable rather than shifting across execution paths.

\section{Design Overview}
\label{sec:design-overview}

\subsection{Core Idea}
\label{subsec:core-idea}

The case study shows that under joint-object modeling, cache misses are both frequent and concentrated in the tail, making them unavoidable and latency-critical. As a result, the system can no longer treat misses as rare events to be hidden, but must explicitly decide how to handle them.

COLoRA is built on a simple principle: a miss should not automatically trigger blocking promotion. Instead, miss handling should be treated as an execution-path decision. For each joint object, the system dynamically chooses between executing from the hot GPU cache or serving the request from the cold layer without waiting.

This principle leads to three requirements: (1) maintaining a precise hot set without inducing cache churn, (2) handling misses without blocking the critical decode path, and (3) overlapping heterogeneous execution so that miss handling does not become the new tail bottleneck.

COLoRA implements these requirements through three corresponding mechanisms: a selective joint-object residency policy, a non-blocking miss-handling path with CPU execution, and an overlap-aware runtime that coordinates GPU hits and CPU misses.

\subsection{Asymmetric Joint-Object Memory Hierarchy}
\label{subsec:memory-hierarchy}

COLoRA manages LoRA residual weights with an asymmetric memory hierarchy. GPU memory is treated as a scarce hot cache that should hold only reusable joint objects. CPU memory holds the complete read-only source pool for all joint objects and therefore acts as both the cold layer and the execution source for fallback. This asymmetry is important because it removes write-back complexity from eviction and ensures that an evicted object remains immediately executable from host memory.

The GPU cache is populated selectively rather than eagerly. Each joint object maintains lightweight utility state derived from recent accesses, and promotion decisions are filtered through minimum-hit thresholds, bounded promotion queues, and cooldown windows. Intuitively, COLoRA promotes objects that show a plausible hot rebound, while suppressing repeated queue traffic for objects that remain cold. This policy is designed to preserve cache precision under the enlarged key space without letting promotion traffic dominate the worker.

\subsection{CPU-First Non-Blocking Miss Handling}
\label{subsec:cpu-first}

On the execution path, COLoRA distinguishes between the dense expert backbone and the sparse LoRA residual. The dense base expert computation remains on GPU. Only the expert-specific LoRA residual is allowed to use the heterogeneous path. This split is crucial because it limits the scope of fallback to the incremental computation that caused the residency problem in the first place, rather than moving the entire MoE layer off GPU.

When a joint object hits in the GPU cache, COLoRA serves it through the regular GPU LoRA path. When it misses, the current request takes a CPU fallback path by default instead of blocking on promotion. The runtime may still enqueue the missed object for promotion, but promotion is treated as an optimization for future requests, not a prerequisite for the current one. This is the central paradigm shift of the design: the system no longer interprets every miss as ``move weight first, execute later.'' It interprets a miss as ``execute now from the cold layer, and only promote if reuse signals justify it.''

\subsection{Low-Overhead CPU Fallback for Sparse Decode Misses}
\label{subsec:cpu-fallback}

The CPU fallback path is explicitly engineered for the small and irregular shapes that appear in decode. Instead of relying only on generic framework operators, COLoRA groups miss work by adapter, uses MoE-specific CPU kernels when available, and keeps the per-miss control path compact. The implementation already exposes AVX-512 BF16 kernels specialized for the gate, up, and down phases of MoE LoRA execution, which matches the paper's requirement that CPU fallback be a viable latency path rather than a correctness-only fallback.

This design choice should be framed carefully in the paper. The claim is not that CPU is generally faster than GPU. The claim is that for cold decode misses with poor reuse, the fixed cost of blocking promotion can exceed the fixed cost of executing the residual directly on CPU. COLoRA wins only if the fallback path stays cheap enough to make that trade favorable on the tail.

\subsection{Overlapped Heterogeneous Execution}
\label{subsec:overlap}

The final piece is overlap. Mixed batches often contain both GPU-cache hits and misses. COLoRA exploits this structure by launching CPU miss work asynchronously when useful GPU hit work is available, then joining the miss result only at the point where the residual output must be merged. This organization lets CPU compute, GPU compute, and host--device movement proceed concurrently when the batch structure allows it.

The runtime also keeps explicit control signals for this path, including promotion queue depth, CPU queue depth, queueing time, overlap ratio, fallback degradations, and promotion-drop causes. These counters matter for an ASPLOS paper because they make the system explainable under load. If COLoRA helps, the paper can attribute the benefit to fewer blocking promotions and better overlap. If it stops helping, the same counters can reveal whether the cause is CPU queue buildup, insufficient GPU hit work, or a pathological cold burst.

\subsection{Expected Benefit and Graceful Degradation}
\label{subsec:graceful-degradation}

COLoRA is not designed to force heterogeneity into every workload. If locality is strong and the active joint objects fit comfortably in GPU memory, the system should naturally behave close to a GPU-only runtime because most requests hit the hot cache and the CPU path rarely triggers. The design matters precisely in the fragmented regime identified by the case study, where cold misses are common enough that a stable miss-time fallback is more valuable than ever more aggressive blocking promotion.


\section{Scope and Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

COLoRA assumes that CPU memory can hold the complete joint-object source pool. This assumption should be stated explicitly because the design depends on a CPU-resident full replica as the cold layer.

COLoRA is most attractive when the workload exhibits a hot--cold split: a reusable GPU-resident head plus a sparse cold tail. If the cold fraction becomes too large, CPU queueing can erode the benefit. Likewise, COLoRA reduces exposure to blocking promotion, but it does not eliminate host--device transfer costs or hardware sensitivity in the CPU path. NUMA placement, CPU vector support, and contention still matter.

\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:evaluation}

We evaluate COLoRA along five dimensions that correspond directly to the claims made in this paper. In particular, we ask the following questions:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{RQ1: End-to-end latency.} Does COLoRA reduce end-to-end decode latency under multi-LoRA workloads?
\item \textbf{RQ2: Tail latency.} How much does COLoRA improve P95/P99 latency under long-tail expert--adapter access patterns?
\item \textbf{RQ3: Miss handling.} How effective is COLoRA's non-blocking miss path, which combines a GPU hot cache with CPU fallback, relative to conventional load-then-run execution?
\item \textbf{RQ4: Component contribution.} What performance gain is attributable to each major component, including CPU fallback and speculative dispatch?
\item \textbf{RQ5: System behavior.} How does COLoRA affect cache hit rate, miss cost, overlap efficiency, and overall resource utilization?
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Hardware and System Configuration}
\label{Configuration}
All experiments are conducted on a single server with the following configuration:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{GPU:} A100 80GB / RTX 6000
\item \textbf{CPU:} Intel Xeon Gold 5520+ (1 socket, 28 physical cores, 56 hardware threads, AVX-512 support)
\item \textbf{Memory:} 376GB RAM
\item \textbf{Interconnect:} PCIe Gen4 / NVLink
\end{itemize}

Unless otherwise noted, the CPU fallback path uses AVX-512-optimized kernels.


\subsection{Models and Workloads}
\label{subsec:workloads}
We instantiate COLoRA on the public \textbf{Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct} checkpoint. Although Qwen3-VL is a multimodal model, our evaluation targets its MoE text decoder because COLoRA operates on decode-time expert--adapter management. The evaluated decoder has 48 layers, hidden size 2048, 128 routed experts per layer, and top-8 routing for each token at every sparse layer. For adapter experiments, we use rank-16 LoRA modules applied to the attention and MLP projections, including the MoE gate, up, and down projections.

All workloads target the decode worker in a PD-separated serving pipeline. We collect real decode-phase routing traces by replaying a fixed corpus of 512 ShareGPT V3 requests through the model and recording the router-selected experts at each token. We then pair this routing stream with semi-realistic adapter-invocation traces derived from the Azure Functions workload trace, which preserves realistic tenant-arrival skew while allowing controlled variation in adapter-side multiplexing.

Unless otherwise specified, we evaluate both independent and correlated tenant-to-adapter mappings and sweep the active adapter cardinality over $\{8, 32, 128\}$. We further vary the decode batch size (typically 1--4) and the request concurrency at the decode worker to test how COLoRA behaves as joint expert--adapter fragmentation and system contention increase together.

\subsection{Baselines}
\label{subsec:baselines}

The main comparison should include an optimized GPU-only baseline that keeps GPU as the only execution target and uses the best available caching and prefetching policy. A second baseline should adopt joint-object cache management but still resolve misses by blocking promotion, which isolates the value of heterogeneous miss handling from the value of finer-grained residency alone. Finally, the paper should include COLoRA ablations, including at least variants without CPU fallback, without asynchronous overlap, and without the optimized MoE CPU kernel path.

\subsection{Tail Latency Reduction}
\label{subsec:tail-lat}

% The evaluation should also expose the runtime mechanics that explain the end-to-end behavior. At minimum, the paper should report cache hit rate and miss breakdown, CPU queue depth and queue wait, CPU compute time, GPU compute time, overlap ratio, promotion-drop breakdown, and host memory footprint. These measurements let the paper demonstrate whether COLoRA improves P99 because it changes miss handling in the intended way, rather than because of an unrelated system effect.

We analyze the impact of COLoRA on tail latency under skewed access patterns.

Under high LoRA concurrency, Naive Offload exhibits significant tail amplification,
with P99 latency increasing sharply.

COLoRA reduces P99 latency by up to X\times.

This is because COLoRA decouples cache miss from request blocking.

Long-tail accesses no longer incur full transfer latency,
but are instead handled via CPU fallback with bounded overhead.

\subsection{Effectiveness of Non-Blocking Miss Handling}
\label{subsec:miss-handling}
We evaluate how COLoRA’s miss handling policy affects system behavior.

Metrics need to report:

miss rate

miss latency

fallback ratio

COLoRA significantly reduces effective miss penalty.

While the miss rate remains similar, the average miss cost decreases by X\%,
as many misses are served via CPU fallback instead of blocking transfers.

This demonstrates that optimizing miss handling policy is as important as improving cache hit rate.

Even when misses are unavoidable, COLoRA ensures they are handled in a non-blocking manner.

COLoRA reduces idle time caused by blocking transfers.

\subsection{Ablation Study}
\label{subsec:ablation}
We evaluate the contribution of each component.

- Full COLoRA
- w/o fallback (always load-then-run)
- w/o speculative dispatch

Removing fallback significantly increases tail latency,
confirming its role in mitigating miss-induced stalls.

Speculative dispatch further improves performance by overlapping CPU and GPU execution.
